claims.text: The initial material is a conventional W–Cu composite formed from tungsten particles and a copper matrix.
Tungsten particles should be coated with a silver layer a few tens of nanometers thick before composite fabrication.
The coating produces a silver interlayer at the W–Cu interface.
The silver interlayer reduces thermal interface resistance between tungsten and copper.
Silver provides a highly thermally conductive bridge across the W–Cu interface.
Silver is chemically compatible with tungsten and copper at the proposed interface.
The silver interlayer facilitates electron and phonon transport across the W–Cu interface.
Keeping the silver interlayer nanoscale prevents degradation of the composite's mechanical properties.
Keeping the silver interlayer nanoscale preserves the composite's irradiation resistance.
Suitable fusion-reactor materials require good thermal conductivity, mechanical durability, and resistance to irradiation.
The proposed benefit should hold under high-temperature operation and moderate irradiation doses typical of fusion-reactor joints.
Relative to an otherwise identical uncoated W–Cu composite, the silver-coated composite will have measurably higher effective thermal conductivity.
Relative to the uncoated baseline, the silver-coated composite will retain comparable mechanical strength.
Relative to the uncoated baseline, the silver-coated composite will retain comparable irradiation resistance.
The beneficial effect depends on optimizing the silver-coating thickness.
An excessively thick silver coating may cause interfacial brittleness.
An excessively thick silver coating may cause unwanted diffusion that compromises mechanical durability.
The magnitude of the thermal-conductivity enhancement is uncertain and requires experimental verification.
The long-term stability of the silver interlayer under irradiation and thermal cycling is uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant conductivity increase, or failure to retain comparable mechanical and irradiation performance, would falsify the hypothesis.
